entry: Frontier conflicts between Native American tribes and European colonial powers, the United States and others in North America, 1609–1890s. Fighting, most often over tribal lands, ran from the 17th century to the end of the 19th. Native confederacies allied with the British in the [[War of 1812]], after which relations were increasingly governed by treaties that transferred large areas of Indigenous land to the United States. The Indian Removal Act of 1830 led to the removal of many Native nations from the Southeast, including along the [[Trail of Tears]]. Native forces often won battles but could not sustain prolonged resistance. The federal government increasingly confined Native peoples to [[Indian reservation|reservations]] across the [[Great Plains]]. Some scholars characterize U.S. policies as [[Genocide|genocide]]; others dispute applying the term to the wars as a whole.

Italian-American organized crime group, also called *Cosa Nostra*, most active in the Northeastern United States. It grew from Italian immigrant neighborhoods in [[New York City]], [[Chicago]] and [[New Orleans]] in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, where Sicilian Mafiosi merged with other Italian criminals. Its basic units are called families, although they are not familial groupings. The Five Families of New York City, the Gambino, Lucchese, Genovese, Bonanno and Colombo families, are the best known, and a body called the Commission coordinates nationwide activity.

Natural history museum on the Upper West Side of [[Manhattan]], New York City. The naturalist Albert S. Bickmore proposed the museum in 1861. It opened in [[Central Park]]'s Arsenal on May 22, 1871, and its first purpose-built structure in Theodore Roosevelt Park opened on December 22, 1877. The complex comprises 21 interconnected buildings with 45 permanent exhibition halls, a planetarium and a library. Its collections contain about 32 million specimens and artifacts, only a small fraction of which can be displayed at any time. The museum has a full-time scientific staff of 225, sponsors over 120 special field expeditions each year and averages about five million visits annually.

Conflict of 1775–1783 between the [[Thirteen Colonies]] and Great Britain, which ended in American independence. The war began with the [[Battles of Lexington and Concord]] in April 1775. The Continental Army, commanded by [[George Washington]], won the decisive [[Siege of Yorktown]] in 1781, after which King George III's government negotiated an end to the war. A Patriot victory at Saratoga in October 1777 convinced France to sign a commercial agreement and a Treaty of Alliance in February 1778. Spain allied with France in 1779 but did not formally ally with the Americans. The [[Treaty of Paris (1783)|Treaty of Paris]], signed September 3, 1783, recognized the sovereignty and independence of the United States. The Treaties of Versailles resolved the conflicts with France and Spain.

Unincorporated territory of the United States in [[Polynesia]], South Pacific (pop., 2024: approximately 47,400). Its largest island, Tutuila, holds the capital, Pago Pago, and the territory has a land area of 77 square miles (199 km²). Europeans first made contact in the 18th century, and the United States took possession in the late 19th century, developing a major naval outpost at the natural harbor of Pago Pago. Since 1967 the territory has had a constitution and republican government, although it remains officially unorganized and is administered by the federal government. Residents are U.S. nationals rather than citizens, and many Samoans oppose birthright citizenship. The U.S. military has a major presence, and tuna products are the main exports.

Large crocodilian reptile native to the Southeastern United States. The species, *Alligator mississippiensis*, is one of two living alligator species and is larger than the Chinese alligator. Adult males measure 3.4 to 4.8 m (11.2 to 15.7 ft) and can weigh up to 450 kg (1,000 lb). An [[Apex predator|apex predator]], it inhabits freshwater wetlands from southern Oklahoma and Texas to North Carolina. Hunting once decimated the population, which was listed under the Endangered Species Act of 1973 and removed from endangered status in 1987. The IUCN classifies it as Least Concern. It is the official state reptile of [[Florida]], [[Louisiana]] and Mississippi.

Bison species endemic to [[North America]], also called the American buffalo. The species, *Bison bison*, is one of two living bison species, along with the European bison. Two subspecies or ecotypes have been described: the smaller plains bison and the larger wood bison, which has a taller, square hump. Wild animals weigh up to 1,270 kg (2,800 lb). The historical range, the great bison belt, spanned from Alaska to the Gulf of Mexico. An estimated population of 60 million in the late 18th century fell to 541 animals by 1889 through commercial hunting and bovine diseases from [[Cattle|domestic cattle]]. Recovery efforts from the mid-20th century reached roughly 31,000 wild bison by March 2019, though most lived in a few national parks and reserves for many years. Reintroductions have restored free-roaming herds in the United States, Canada and Mexico. Indigenous peoples of the [[Great Plains]] relied on the bison for food, hides and tools, and the species is the national mammal of the United States.

Medium-sized bear endemic to [[North America]], the continent's smallest and most widely distributed bear species. The species, *Ursus americanus*, is an omnivore whose diet varies greatly by season and location. It mainly inhabits forested regions but may venture beyond them, and individuals are occasionally drawn to human settlements by accessible food. The IUCN lists it as least concern because of its wide distribution and a population estimated to be twice that of all other bear species combined. Along with the brown bear, it is one of two modern bear species not considered globally threatened.

Large [[Amphibian|amphibian]] of the family Ranidae, native to eastern North America. The species, *Lithobates catesbeianus*, typically inhabits large permanent water bodies such as swamps, ponds and lakes. Its name comes from the male's breeding call, which sounds like a bull bellowing. It is a generalist carnivore, and it is eaten by alligators, snakes and birds. It is commercially harvested for meat, especially in the southern United States. The bullfrog has been introduced to more than 40 countries, where it is considered an [[Invasive species|invasive species]] because of its voracious appetite and the large number of eggs it produces, which harm native amphibians, insects and other fauna.

Team sport contested by two teams of 11 players on a rectangular field with goalposts at each end. The offense has four downs to advance the ball at least 10 yards, or it turns the ball over to the defense. Teams score by carrying or throwing the ball into the opposing end zone for a touchdown or by kicking a field goal. The sport evolved in the [[United States]] from soccer and rugby, and the first game was played on November 6, 1869, between Rutgers and Princeton. Rule changes drawn up by Walter Camp from 1880 established the line of scrimmage, the snap and the downs system. The National Football League governs the professional game, whose championship, the Super Bowl, is among the most-watched club sporting events globally. Concerns about chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a degenerative brain disease tied to repeated head trauma, have led to rule changes; it was found in 91.7% of 376 examined former NFL players' brains at autopsy.

Historical region of the advancing margin of European-American settlement westward across North America, c. 1607–1912. The frontier began with European colonial settlements in the early 17th century and ended with the admission of the last contiguous western territories as states in 1912. The U.S. Census Bureau declared the frontier closed in 1890. Settlement was encouraged by [[Thomas Jefferson]] after the [[Louisiana Purchase]] of 1803, which gave rise to the expansionist idea of [[Manifest destiny|manifest destiny]]. Trails such as the Cumberland Gap, opened by [[Daniel Boone]] in the 1770s, and the 1849 California Gold Rush drew migrants, and expansion displaced Native populations through treaties and warfare. [[Frederick Jackson Turner]] argued that the frontier was formative to American democracy and individualism. Its legends, known as the frontier myth, shaped the [[Western (genre)|Western genre]] of media, which remains part of American national identity.

Migratory [[Thrush (bird)|thrush]] of North America, named after the [[European robin]] for its reddish-orange breast. The two species are not closely related, since the European robin belongs to the [[Old World flycatcher]] family. The American robin is widely distributed across North America and winters from southern Canada to central Mexico. According to the Partners in Flight database (2019), it is the most abundant landbird in North America, with 370 million individuals, and it has seven subspecies. The species is active mostly during the day and forages on invertebrates such as earthworms and caterpillars, and on fruits and berries. It is among the earliest birds to lay eggs, beginning to breed shortly after returning to its summer range. The main predator of adults is the domestic cat. Brown-headed cowbirds lay eggs in robin nests, but the robins usually reject them.

Landmass comprising [[North America]] and [[South America]], the second largest continent by area after [[Asia]]. The Americas cover 8% of Earth's total surface area and 28.4% of its land area. The American Cordillera runs the length of the west coast, while the flatter east is dominated by large river basins such as the Amazon and Mississippi. Humans first settled the Americas from Asia between 20,000 and 16,000 years ago. Following the voyages of [[Christopher Columbus]] from 1492 to 1504, the [[Columbian exchange]] began, and diseases introduced from Europe and West Africa devastated Indigenous populations. Decolonization began with the [[American Revolution]] and largely ended with the [[Spanish–American War]] in the late 1890s. The Americas have more than a billion inhabitants, two-thirds of whom live in the United States, Brazil and Mexico. The name derives from [[Amerigo Vespucci]].

Synthetic radioactive chemical element, symbol Am and atomic number 95, in the actinide series. It was first produced in 1944 at the University of Chicago's Metallurgical Laboratory during the [[Manhattan Project]], by a team led by Glenn T. Seaborg, and its discovery was kept secret until November 1945. It was named after the [[Americas]] by analogy with [[Europium|europium]], which lies above it in the periodic table. Most americium is produced when uranium or plutonium is bombarded with neutrons in nuclear reactors; one tonne of spent nuclear fuel contains about 100 grams. Its most common isotope, americium-241, has a half-life of 432.2 years. Americium is used in ionization chamber smoke detectors, neutron sources and industrial gauges.

Italian explorer and navigator from the Republic of [[Florence]], after whom the [[Americas]] are named. Vespucci took part in voyages between 1499 and 1502, first for Spain and then for Portugal. Booklets published under his name in 1503 and 1505 described these voyages and were widely read in Europe, though historians dispute their authorship and accuracy. In 1501 he wrote that Brazil was part of a fourth continent unknown to Europeans, which he called the [[New World]] (*Mundus Novus*). In 1507 the cartographer Martin Waldseemüller applied the Latinized name *America* to a map of the New World, and other cartographers followed. In 1508 Vespucci was appointed piloto mayor, or master navigator, of Spain's Casa de Contratación in [[Seville]].

Violet variety of [[Quartz]]. Its color comes from trace iron impurities. Its name derives from an [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] word meaning not intoxicated, reflecting the ancient belief that it prevented drunkenness. Major deposits occur in [[Brazil]], [[Uruguay]] and [[Zambia]], usually in cavities within volcanic rock. With a Mohs hardness of 7, amethyst is used in jewelry and is the traditional birthstone for February. Large Brazilian discoveries in the 19th century increased supply and reduced its rarity.

Ethio-Semitic language of the [[Afroasiatic languages|Afroasiatic]] family, spoken chiefly in [[Ethiopia]]. It is the first language of the Amhara people and a [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] for other populations in Ethiopia. It is the official working language of the federal government and of several federal regions. Amharic had over 33.7 million mother-tongue speakers in 2020, and the total number of speakers exceeds 58.8 million. It is the second most widely spoken [[Semitic languages|Semitic]] language after [[Arabic]]. It is written left to right in the Ethiopic script, or *fidäl*, an abugida in which consonant-vowel sequences are written as units. There is no universally agreed Romanization into [[Latin script|Latin script]].

Organic compound of the general formula R−C(=O)−NR′R″, derived from a [[Carboxylic acid|carboxylic acid]] by replacing its hydroxyl group with an amino group. Common amides include formamide, acetamide and benzamide. Amides are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary according to the number of acyl groups bonded to the nitrogen atom. The amide group is planar and only weakly basic, and its hydrogen bonding raises the boiling and melting points of amides above those of hydrocarbons of similar weight. Amide bonds join [[Amino acid|amino acids]] into [[Protein|proteins]] as peptide bonds, and amides form the backbone of synthetic polymers such as [[Nylon]].

Family of [[Personal computer|personal computers]] produced by Commodore from 1985 until the company's bankruptcy in 1994. The Amiga used custom chips to accelerate graphics and sound and ran the multitasking AmigaOS [[Operating system|operating system]] with a desktop environment called Workbench. The Amiga 1000 was released in July 1985. The Amiga 500, introduced in 1987, became the bestselling model. Its strength in audio, multimedia and video games made it popular as a home computer, and many [[Video game|video games]] originated on it. Commodore is estimated to have sold nearly five million Amigas.

Organic compound derived from [[Ammonia]], in which one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups. Amines are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary according to whether one, two or three carbon groups are attached to the nitrogen atom. The nitrogen atom has a lone pair of electrons, and amines are basic, with basicity similar to that of ammonia. The amino group, −NH₂, is the functional group of primary amines. The simplest aromatic amine, aniline, consists of a [[Benzene|benzene]] ring bonded to an amino group. Amines are building blocks of [[Amino acid|amino acids]] and components of [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitters]] such as [[Dopamine]] and [[Serotonin]].

Organic compound containing both [[Amine|amino]] and [[Carboxylic acid|carboxylic acid]] functional groups. Over 500 amino acids occur in nature, but the α-amino acids incorporated into [[Protein|proteins]] are by far the most important, and only these appear in the [[Genetic code|genetic code]]. Amino acids link through peptide bonds to form polypeptides and, ultimately, proteins. Nine amino acids are essential for humans, meaning the body cannot synthesize them and they must come from the diet: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine. Amino acids also serve as precursors of neurotransmitters; tryptophan, for example, is the precursor of serotonin.

Indo-Persian Sufi singer, musician, court poet and scholar of the [[Delhi Sultanate]]. He was a disciple of the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya of Delhi and served seven successive rulers of the Delhi Sultanate. He wrote mainly in Persian, also in Hindavi and Punjabi, and his output exceeded 90 works, including five divans of [[Ghazal|ghazals]] and the *Khamsa*, a quintet emulating [[Nizami Ganjavi]]. He is regarded as the father of qawwali, a devotional form of [[Sufism|Sufi]] singing, and he introduced the ghazal style of song into India. He is also credited with innovating forms such as tarana and khayal and with inventing the sitar and tabla, though some attributions blend legend with history. He earned the title *Tuti-e-Hind*, or Parrot of India.

Traditionalist Anabaptist Christian church fellowships of Swiss and Alsatian origin. The Amish church began with a schism led by Jakob Ammann among Swiss and Alsatian [[Mennonites]] in 1693. Amish life emphasizes plain dress, simple living, pacifism and separation from the wider world. Church members follow a code of rules called the *Ordnung*, reviewed twice a year. Old Order Amish schools typically end after eighth grade. As of 2024, about 415,000 Old Order Amish lived in the United States and over 6,000 in Canada.

Indian actor, playback singer and film producer who works primarily in [[Hindi]] cinema. Bachchan was born in Allahabad (now [[Prayagraj]]). He has starred in over 200 films and has received seven National Film Awards, including a record four for Best Actor. In the 1970s he became known as the Angry Young Man for roles in films such as *Zanjeer* (1973) and *Deewaar* (1975). [[François Truffaut]] described him as a one-man industry. Bachchan received the Padma Shri in 1984, the Padma Bhushan in 2001 and the Padma Vibhushan in 2015, and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, India's highest cinematic honor. He hosted several seasons of the game show *Kaun Banega Crorepati*, the Indian version of *Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?*

Tricyclic antidepressant used chiefly to treat [[Major depressive disorder|major depressive disorder]] and pain syndromes. It was discovered by Merck in the late 1950s and approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 1961. It is on the [[World Health Organization|World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines and is generally considered second-line therapy because of frequent side effects, including dry mouth, drowsiness, dizziness, constipation and weight gain. It increases levels of [[Serotonin|serotonin]] and norepinephrine in the brain by inhibiting their reuptake. In 2023 it was the 90th most commonly prescribed medication in the U.S., with more than 7 million prescriptions.
